title: NeoVolta Q&A: Transforming Energy Storage into a Grid Asset
content:
Stationary Batteries
Industry Outlook
Interviews
NeoVolta Q&A: Transforming Energy Storage into a Grid Asset
NeoVolta's CEO shares insights on battery storage technology, highlighting its potential to become a reliable, essential asset for the future energy grid.
Jake Hertz
May 20, 2026
5 Min Read
NeoVolta’s NV Wave modular click-in residential ESS.
Courtesy of Neovolta.
With global battery storage installations jumping by 43% in 2025 and in the US hitting record growth, the industry conversation is shifting from simple solar-pairing to treating storage as the primary grid asset. Ardes Johnson, CEO of
NeoVolta,
believes that the next phase of the energy transition belongs to "firm power", or dispatchable capacity that can move beyond backup power to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs) and demand response programs.
NeoVolta is a US-based manufacturer specializing in residential and commercial energy storage solutions designed for immediate, build-ready execution. While many competitors remain buried in long-term R&D, NeoVolta has focused on high-fidelity integration of
lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) chemistry
and intelligent load management. By avoiding the price volatility of cobalt and nickel and centering their strategy on domestic manufacturing, the company is positioning itself to align with the domestic content requirements of the
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
(OBBBA) .
Battery Technology
interviewed Johnson to learn about NeoVolta and their vision for using residential batteries as proactive, grid-stabilizing assets.
Related:
Advancing Energy Infrastructure with a Modular Nuclear Energy Platform
Ardes Johnson, CEO of NeoVolta.
With global battery storage installations jumping by 43% in 2025 and record growth in the US, how is NeoVolta positioning its systems to capture this immediate surge in demand compared to long-term R&D competitors?
Ardes Johnson, CEO of NeoVolta:
NeoVolta has focused on delivering relevant products that serve multiple markets without overcomplicating the choices for installers or end-users. That approach has given us the breathing room to watch how the market is evolving and build systems that not only meet today’s demand but help set the standard for what customers should expect in this category.
Importantly, we don’t view this as a hardware race alone. Software, data visibility, installer experience, and homeowner usability are all critical to launching a complete energy platform rather than simply shipping another piece of equipment. As storage adoption accelerates, the companies that succeed will be the ones delivering a well-rounded solution — not just a product — and that has been NeoVolta’s design philosophy from the start.
How is NeoVolta navigating the OBBBA and domestic content requirements to keep your residential and light commercial systems eligible for federal investment tax credits?
Johnson:
Our strategy around domestic manufacturing predates the OBBBA. NeoVolta has long planned to establish US-based manufacturing across the full storage spectrum — from residential systems through the often underserved commercial and
industrial “middle market,” and into utility-scale storage.
Related:
Five Key Takeaways on Ford Energy's Bold BESS Market Entry
The OBBBA effectively accelerated a roadmap that was already underway. That momentum
led to the announcement of NeoVolta Power, our 2 GWh battery energy storage
manufacturing facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, which will produce both front-of-the-meter
and behind-the-meter solutions for utility and C&I markets.
On the residential side, we’ve also evolved select systems to align with OBBBA guidance and emerging domestic content frameworks. Those compliance formulas have been designed directly into our next generation of residential products, which will launch this summer.
As the industry moves toward “firm power” and dispatchable capacity, how are your battery systems specifically engineered to participate in the new market structures for demand response and virtual power plants?
Johnson:
The industry conversation is shifting from simply pairing solar with storage to recognizing that storage itself is the primary grid asset, with solar as an optional generation source layered on top. NeoVolta designs its systems with that philosophy in mind. Our batteries are engineered to function as controllable grid resources capable of participating in demand response, time-of-use optimization, and virtual power plant aggregation as those market structures continue to expand.
Related:
AI Data Centers Stretch Tech Innovation Limits
By starting with storage as the foundation and integrating intelligent load management and software coordination, we enable systems that provide both end-user resilience and dispatchable capacity that utilities and aggregators can rely on. That dual value proposition will become increasingly important as distributed batteries begin contributing more meaningfully to grid stability.
Do you see NeoVolta’s distributed, smaller-scale distribution-sited batteries helping to shorten deployment timelines by bypassing current grid constraints?
Johnson:
Distributed storage absolutely has the potential to accelerate deployment timelines, particularly compared to large centralized infrastructure projects that may require lengthy transmission upgrades.
But creating the product alone is not enough. What truly shortens deployment timelines is building the ecosystem around it. That means working with developers, community choice aggregators, utilities, and program operators that need reliable technology partners and a consistent supply of systems to scale their programs.
When those partnerships are in place, distributed batteries can be deployed much faster and closer to load centers. That creates a model where program operators can scale their offerings while manufacturers like NeoVolta scale production — ultimately leading to faster and more predictable deployment across the grid.
Given the downward trend in global battery prices and potential short-term volatility in raw materials, what is NeoVolta’s strategy to stay economically competitive while building a resilient domestic supply chain?
Johnson:
Cost competitiveness and supply chain resilience have to be addressed simultaneously. While battery prices have declined globally, the industry also recognizes the risks of overdependence on concentrated supply chains and critical minerals.
NeoVolta’s strategy is to pair efficient product design with a growing domestic manufacturing footprint. Our use of lithium iron phosphate chemistry helps avoid exposure to nickel and cobalt volatility, while our US assembly platform improves logistics, quality control, and alignment with domestic content incentives.
At the same time, we’re not only planning for what the supply chain needs today. We’re preparing for where policy and market requirements are headed. As domestic content thresholds and FEOC requirements increase over time, we anticipate the industry moving further upstream. NeoVolta is already evaluating the long-term path toward deeper vertical integration, including the eventual potential for domestic battery cell manufacturing.

title: Battery Swapping Products Drive Innovation in Construction
content:
Battery Applications
Portable
Industry Outlook
Trends
News
Battery Swapping Products Drive Innovation in Construction
Swappable battery technology enhances construction equipment reliability, reduces downtime, and supports zero-emission solutions for demanding jobsite applications.
Maria Guerra
,
Senior Editor-Battery Technology
,
Informa Markets
May 20, 2026
3 Min Read
Swappable battery technology products transform the construction industry.
Vanguard.
Battery-swapping technology is now widespread across industries, from electric vehicles (EVs) to construction equipment. In the automotive sector,
EV battery swapping
offers a practical solution to range anxiety by enabling drivers to replace depleted batteries with fully charged ones in minutes, rather than waiting for lengthy recharging times. This same principle is now applied to other industries, where uninterrupted operation is critical. By allowing users to quickly swap batteries, this innovation minimizes downtime, simplifies power management, and enhances productivity, making it an ideal choice for applications that demand efficiency and reliability.
Applications for construction and surface preparation
In the construction and surface preparation industries, where equipment reliability and uptime are paramount, swappable battery technology is proving to be a game-changer.
Bartell Global
, in partnership with
Vanguard
, is leveraging the innovative 48V 1.5kWh Commercial Swappable Battery Pack (Si1.5) to power three new additions to its equipment lines: the B424 Edger Trowel, BC436 Power Trowel, and BCF1570 Forward Plate Compactor. These battery-powered solutions enable power swapping across different machines. As Matt Locke, VP of Sales – The Americas at Bartell Global, states, “By adopting this unified, swappable ecosystem, we are simplifying the jobsite experience — reducing the need for multiple chargers and parts while allowing crews to easily swap power across different machine types.”
Related:
SoftBank’s Zinc-Halogen Batteries Challenge LFP in AI Data Centers
The partnership between these two companies marks a significant step forward in integrating swappable battery technology into professional-grade equipment. Therefore, ensuring that contractors can easily transport and maneuver equipment while maintaining the energy required for demanding applications. Additionally, the Si1.5 is backed by engineering expertise, product support, and an 8-year limited commercial warranty, providing long-term confidence for dealers, rental partners, and contractors alike.
Vanguard Si1.5 battery pack design
The Vanguard Si1.5 battery pack is designed to meet the high-productivity demands of modern jobsites. According to the company, Its fast-charging capability — reaching 80% charge in approximately 50 minutes — allows operators to recharge during natural breaks, such as lunch or travel time, effectively eliminating downtime. This maintenance-free battery is engineered and assembled in the USA, ensuring reliability and durability for commercial use. By integrating this technology into Bartell Global’s equipment, contractors gain access to zero-emission solutions that are ideal for noise-sensitive and enclosed environments, such as schools, hospitals, and residential areas.
Related:
From Apollo to Artemis II: Batteries in Space!
48V 1.5kWh commercial battery swappable battery pack. Courtesy of Vanguard.
Standardizing battery swappable platforms
Bartell Global’s adoption of the Vanguard Si1.5 battery pack reflects its commitment to evolving with industry needs. By centering its electric portfolio around a standardized, swappable power platform, the company is creating a scalable foundation for future innovation. This approach allows Bartell Global to expand battery integration across additional equipment lines, including compaction, concrete finishing, and surface preparation platforms. As Matt Locke, VP of Sales – The Americas at Bartell Global, notes, “By adopting this unified, swappable ecosystem, we are simplifying the jobsite experience — reducing the need for multiple chargers and parts while allowing crews to easily swap power across different machine types.”
Swappable battery technology is set to transform the construction industry by enabling greater efficiency, sustainability, and adaptability on jobsites. As lithium-ion battery prices fall, this innovation is becoming more accessible, allowing contractors to integrate electric solutions into their workflows. As demand for zero-emission equipment grows, advancements in battery capacity and portability will further reduce downtime and support the industry's shift toward greener practices, ensuring that swappable batteries become a vital component of construction's future.

content:

Solid-State Batteries: The Battery Show Europe Plots the Path to Scale
Explore solid-state battery readiness, challenges, and Europe’s strategy for scaling this transformative EV technology.
Dan Carney
,
Senior Editor
,
Design News
May 19, 2026
2 Min Read
Mercedes-Benz solid-state battery logo.
Dan Carney
At a Glance
Assess solid-state battery maturity and readiness
Learn commercialization timelines and bottlenecks
Compare solid-state to lithium-ion and alternatives
One of the biggest questions facing the global auto industry is when
solid-state batteries
will arrive in scale. This will be a transformative event that makes EVs even more economically attractive and could be the necessary step to permit the sunsetting of combustion power.
Attendees to
The Battery Show Europe 2026
at Messe Stuttgart, June 9-11, can get an update on progress toward this long-sought goal in the session, “
Solid-State Batteries Beyond the Hype: Readiness, Reality and Europe’s Path to Scale
” on Wednesday, June 10
th
.  You can sign up here:
Registration
.
The three panelists in this session will discuss the fact that while solid-state batteries are frequently positioned as the next major breakthrough in EV performance, safety, and energy density, commercial deployment has remained stubbornly out of reach despite years of investment and announcements. The panel will look at where solid-state technology genuinely stands today, separating technical reality from long-term ambition.
The discussion will assess what has changed, what challenges still block scale-up, and how solid-state fits into Europe’s broader mobility, industrial, and policy objectives. They will also question whether solid-state is the right near-term bet, or whether alternative chemistries may deliver impact sooner.
They promise three outcomes to benefit attendees:
A realistic assessment of solid-state technical maturity, manufacturing readiness, and remaining bottlenecks
Clear-eyed timelines for commercialization and what would need to change to accelerate them
How solid-state compares to advanced lithium-ion and emerging alternatives in terms of cost, scale, and strategic fit for Europe

title: EV Supply Chain Needs Strong EV Government Support
content:
EV Batteries
Battery Manufacturing
Industry Outlook
Trends
EV Supply Chain Needs Strong Government Support
Lotus Technology Inc.’s struggles in battery manufacturing highlight the urgent need for EV government support to boost the EV supply chain.
Maria Guerra
,
Senior Editor-Battery Technology
,
Informa Markets
May 19, 2026
3 Min Read
Emeya is Lotus’ first electric hyper-GT.
Courtesy of Lotus.
The push to establish a robust electric vehicle (EV) supply chain has highlighted the indispensable role of government support in fostering innovation, securing investments, and ensuring long-term sustainability. The challenges faced by Lotus Technology Inc., as reported by
Bloomberg
, underscore the urgent need for strategic government intervention to secure the future of the EV sector.
Lotus Technology’s EV battery struggles in Europe
Lotus
, owned by China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Group, is struggling to find a European partner to build EV batteries. This partnership would help the company localize production and comply with the European Union’s complex content rules. “In China, you may instantly find five to six right partners,” stated Lotus CEO Qingfeng Feng in an interview with Bloomberg. “But in the EU it simply didn’t work as we expect.” This bold contrast highlights the lack of established battery manufacturing infrastructure in the UK and Europe, leaving companies like Lotus at a disadvantage.
Related:
Upstream Monitoring Redefines EV Battery Quality Control
Europe’s efforts to build a competitive EV supply chain are under pressure. The collapse of battery startups such as Britishvolt and
Northvolt
has further exposed the fragility of the region’s EV battery ambitions.
Learning from the Britishvolt bankruptcy
Britishvolt, once a symbol of the UK’s EV aspirations,
filed for administration in 2023
after failing to secure sufficient private investment. The company had planned to build a $3.9B gigafactory in Northumberland, which would have produced 300,000 battery cells annually and created thousands of jobs. However, despite an initial government grant and agreements with automakers like Lotus, Britishvolt’s lack of a clear sales strategy and financial backing led to its downfall.
Lotus had previously agreed to a deal with Britishvolt, but the startup’s collapse has left the luxury automaker scrambling for alternatives. This situation underscores the need for reliable funding and stronger government support to reduce risks in high-stakes EV ventures.
The role of government support
Lotus is not solely focusing on EVs; it is also investing in hybrid technology as part of its strategy to navigate the evolving automotive landscape. The company plans to produce plug-in hybrid versions of the Emira and a new hybrid supercar, the Type 135, at its Hethel factory near Norwich. This dual focus reflects an approach to meeting diverse market demands while managing production costs and regulatory challenges.
Meanwhile, many years ago, China’s government started adopting a strategic approach to battery dominance. Galyen Energy’s Robert (Bob) Galyen, former CTO of Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL), highlighted at the latest Battery Show North America that
China’s systematic approach to battery dominance
has government support as one of its principal pillars, including robust subsidies, guaranteed purchases of early, expensive technology, and the fostering of a domestic supply chain. This has positioned China as a global leader in battery innovation and production.
Related:
Subaru’s 2026 Solterra EV Touring XT Delivers Power, Range, & Mixed Ride Quality
Lotus is seeking investment from the UK government to support its Hethel factory near Norwich. “Our team is currently actively making feasibility studies and investigating the potential solutions,” Feng told Bloomberg. “However, we would also like to get some help and support from the UK government.” This plea for public funding highlights the critical role of government intervention in fostering a sustainable EV ecosystem.
Without the government’s sustained, strategic support, countries risk falling further behind in the race for EV dominance. Lotus’s current challenges serve as an absolute reminder of the critical role government support plays in building a competitive EV supply chain.

title: Battery Safety, Thermal Management at Battery Show Europe 2026
content:
Thermal Management
Testing & Safety
News
Thermal Management & Safety Issues Under Scope at The Battery Show Europe
Technical sessions examine safety challenges and thermal management innovations that are critical to battery cells and stationary battery systems.
Spencer Chin
,
Senior Editor
,
Design News
May 19, 2026
4 Min Read
Battery cell and system thermal and safety issues will be the focus of several sessions at The Battery Show Europe.
Battery Show Europe
Battery fires and outright failures are an unfortunate reality that engineers are trying to lessen in future battery cells. At the upcoming
The Battery Show Europe
in Stuttgart, Germany June 9 through 11, several sessions will look at the progress being made to resolve long-standing issues such as thermal runaway and cell microcracking. Here are several sessions anyone concerned about battery safety and reliability should attend.
Designing Thermal Management and Safety into Battery Packs for Next-Generation Batteries
https://tbse26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=167
Thursday, 11 June
2:30 PM - 3:00 PM CET
As battery chemistries evolve, pack-level thermal management and safety strategies must adapt to new operating profiles, mechanical behaviours and failure modes. While next-generation cells promise improvements in intrinsic safety and performance, they also introduce new design challenges that can only be addressed through collaborative innovation in structural design and materials.
This session uses a next-generation battery pack development program as a case study to examine how thermal management, containment and structural design choices are changing at pack level. The focus is on the engineering rationale behind key design decisions, the trade-offs encountered during testing and validation, and the lessons learned when balancing thermal protection, weight and manufacturability.
Cathode Microcracking: Understanding and Preventing Long-Term Degradation in Commercial Cells
https://tbse26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=42
Tuesday, 9 June
2:00 PM - 3:00 PM CET
As the push for energy density drives increases in the nickel content of NMC and NCA cathodes, mechanical stress and microcracking has become a major challenge that can lead to non-linear degradation and rollover failure. As service lifetimes of EV batteries and BESS systems continually improve, long-term degradation studies are needed that assess the effectiveness of strategies to prevent microcracking over thousands of cycles and decades of service life.  This presentation uses advanced x-ray imaging and diffraction to characterize the surprising long-term effects of microcracking in commercially manufactured pouch cells that have been extensively cycled in Dr. Jeff Dahn’s lab at Dalhousie University. The presentation will show how operating conditions and materials selection can dramatically impact the extent of microcracking, including a remarkable single-crystal cell that has been cycled more than 20,000 times over a period of 6 years.
From Propagation to Prevention: Materials Solutions for Improved Battery Safety
https://tbse26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=225
Tuesday, 9 June
1:00 PM - 1:45 PM CET
This session will discuss the challenge of maintaining battery safety while reducing design constraints at the module level, and will explore materials-based solutions for mitigating risks such as thermal runaway propagation, pressure control and ingress management. Details around testing under real-world conditions will be presented and discussed.
BESS Safety: Trends in Thermal Management, Fire & Explosion Protection
https://tbse26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=196
Wednesday, 10 June
12:15 PM - 12:30 PM CET
Amid several high-profile stationary battery energy storage system (BESS) fire incidents, scrutiny of BESS safety has intensified in recent years. Risks to personnel, financial losses, asset damage, and environmental impact are all driving demand for safer Li-ion BESS technologies.
As the German market shifts from a predominantly behind-the-meter (BTM) focus toward larger utility-scale projects, developers and integrators must prepare for the expansion of European supply chains for thermal management, fire protection, and explosion mitigation materials and components. In parallel, the rapid growth of data centers across Germany and Europe will place greater emphasis on deploying safer BESS technologies at hyperscale facilities. By applying lessons learned from past safety incidents, stakeholders can help safeguard Germany’s market from large-scale BESS safety events that could otherwise hinder domestic growth.
Increasing Risk of Aged Cells – A Comparison of Cell Chemistries
https://tbse26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=109
Tuesday, 9 June
3:30 PM - 4:00 PM CET
This sessions will overview the safety aspects of lithium-ion cells with the typical sequence of a thermal runaway. Presentation of research results how the risk of a thermal runaway is increasing over lifetime due to degradation for different cell chemistries like NMC, LFP and LTO. Safety standards and test often do not always consider this aspect of growing risk.
How To Design Simulate and Homologate IEC62619 With NMC Cells: Thermal Runaway in Railway Applications
https://tbse26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=112
Thursday, 11 June
2:00 PM - 2:30 PM CET
As regulatory scrutiny around battery safety intensifies, pack developers must demonstrate not only performance but controlled failure behaviour. Thermal runaway containment is no longer a laboratory concern but a certification requirement, particularly in transport sectors with strict homologation standards such as rail.
This session will examine how early-stage 3D multiphysics simulation, combined with incremental physical testing, can de-risk battery pack design by predicting and validating thermal propagation behavior in high-energy NMC systems. Using 100 kWh HEV pack architecture as a case study, the presentation will outline how numerical modelling and experimental correlation inform safer material and structural decisions.

title: ProLogium CEO Shares Insights on Solid-State Battery Leadership
content:
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Battery Manufacturing
Interviews
ProLogium CEO Shares Insights on Solid-State Battery Leadership
Vincent Yang, CEO of ProLogium, discusses solid-state battery advancements, manufacturing strategies, and the future of energy storage.
Maria Guerra
,
Senior Editor-Battery Technology
,
Informa Markets
May 18, 2026
6 Min Read
ProLogium’s solid-state battery cell.
Courtesy of ProLogium.
In this interview with Battery Technology, Vincent Yang, CEO of
ProLogium
, discusses advancements in solid-state battery technology, key manufacturing strategies, and the company's vision for the future of energy storage.
ProLogium has achieved volume production of solid-state batteries while many competitors remain in the lab. What were the key technological breakthroughs or strategic decisions that enabled ProLogium to reach this milestone ahead of others?
Vincent Yang, Founder & CEO of ProLogium:
We attribute our progress to our long-term strategy focused on innovation and manufacturing capabilities since ProLogium’s inception two decades ago.
Our uniqueness is built on the full integration of two critical components. We developed a superfluidized all-inorganic electrolyte, made without rare elements, that achieves world-record conductivity and features an Active Safety Mechanism (ASM) that automatically decomposes to eliminate fire risk at the material level.
Related:
Toshiba’s SCiB Battery Comparison with Conventional Li-ion Batteries
We paired this with a highly stable ceramic separator that prevents the charged cathode and anode from making contact, thereby stopping dangerous thermal chain reactions. Underpinned by this triple safety, high energy density can be continuously pursued from the chemical level and system, with reactive cathode and anode active materials like NMC 955, silicon-based anode, and Li-metal.
Our approach is also more cost competitive. With silicon anode unit energy cost at two-thirds that of graphite, and proprietary electrolyte synthesis cost approaching parity with liquid electrolytes, and dry room requirements of 30%-40% of a conventional EV battery, production is more efficient and cost effective. Strategically, our key tactics have been to prove our manufacturing readiness in parallel with our R&D. We have re-engineered how solid-state batteries are manufactured — eliminating the most complex and time-consuming steps in conventional battery production to achieve structural advantages in cost, speed, and throughput.
For example, we reduced the core production process from 17 to 11 steps by eliminating separator film placement, liquid electrolyte injection, vacuum soaking, and degassing. Our proprietary hot flow dehydration takes 8 minutes versus 8 hours compared to traditional processes. While others remained in the lab, still struggling to overcome high manufacturing costs and the need for external pressure during operation, ProLogium has already addressed these challenges with shipment of over 2.4 million cells to date. This includes approximately 800,000 cells delivered from our new GWh-class production line in Taiwan since it came online in Q3 2024.
Related:
Latest LFP Battery Projects Driving Safety, Sustainability, and Savings
With the new gigafactory in Dunkirk, France, how does ProLogium plan to strengthen the global battery supply chain? What role will this facility play in meeting the growing demand for EV batteries and other applications?
Yang:
The Dunkirk gigafactory is a cornerstone of our global expansion strategy and a direct response to Europe's push for a resilient, sovereign battery supply chain. This facility is purpose-built for mass-production of our fourth-generation superfluidized inorganic battery for the European and global market, applying the proven manufacturing framework from our operational gigafactory in Taiwan.
The first fab will feature a production capacity of 4 GWh a year, rising gradually to 12 GWh upon the completion of Phase 2. The Dunkirk site will establish a local manufacturing system—covering production, quality, and supply-chain collaboration—designed around an all-inorganic solid-state electrolyte architecture to balance safety, performance, and manufacturability at scale. The new plant will be integrated into the broader "Battery Valley" in Northern France, allowing us to leverage a rich ecosystem of talent, materials, recycling, and technology partners.
Related:
Hawaii's 'Maui Method' Transforms Lithium-Ion Battery Disposal, Earns EPA Endorsement
By localizing production with the strong backing of the French government—including a historic €1.5 billion subsidy—and utilizing the region's low-carbon, clean power, we are building a European manufacturing backbone to reliably meet the growing demand for not only EV batteries but a wide range of other applications that require safer, higher-performance energy.
Rendering of the Dunkirk gigafactory. Courtesy of ProLogium.
ProLogium is adapting its solid-state technology for applications beyond EVs, such as data centers, aerospace, and energy storage systems. What are the unique challenges and opportunities in these sectors, and how does ProLogium plan to address them?
Yang:
Emerging industries like aerospace, AI infrastructure, robotics, mobile energy, and defense are driving new battery demands beyond EVs. Next-gen batteries must offer high energy density, safety, extreme environment performance, balanced efficiency, and cost-effectiveness to meet these needs.
Intrinsic safety is a key feature of our technology that is required by many of these emerging applications given the high value-add nature of these industries. Meanwhile, each industry has unique system-level requirements. For example, battery weight is important for aerospace applications such as aircraft, eVTOL, satellite and drones where customers are looking for batteries that are 30-50% lighter for the same capacity.
In ESS (energy storage systems), 2x to 5x power capability and low heat generation are critical in ensuring optimal performance and cost effectiveness at data centers. For robotics, longer mission runtime and faster charging speeds are highly desired. Our strategy addresses this through a partner-led model. We focus on manufacturing the most technically demanding part—the core internal cell—which our domain-specialist partners then handle for final system integration and deployment.
For example, our partnership with Delta Electronics is focused on developing battery management systems for energy storage and AI data centers, while our collaboration with Kyushu Electric Power is creating specialized modules for zero-emission construction equipment. This partner-driven ecosystem strategy is similar to how we work with Tier 1 partners such as Rimac and FEV in the EV market — leveraging their platforms and integration capabilities to showcase the strengths of our battery cells, bring them into end-customer EV platforms, and accelerate market penetration.
While tariffs have significantly influenced the production and supply chain of LFP batteries, how are they affecting the development and adoption of next-generation technologies like solid-state batteries? Are there specific policy changes that could accelerate innovation and global deployment?
Yang:
Tariffs have not meaningfully impacted our production and supply chain. Overall, our strategy is designed to build a resilient global supply chain that is less vulnerable to regional dependency. No LFP cathode or graphite anode is used in our chemistry. Instead, our battery chemistry, which does not use rare materials, allows for greater supply chain resilience, especially for customers who are looking for alternative battery supply options.
There is an imbalance in terms of policy support for battery innovation across different markets. During an age where energy resilience and industrial sovereignty are top of mind, there are opportunities for public and private players to work together and push innovation forward in the battery space. The French government's "France 2030" plan, which is backing our Dunkirk project, is a great example. This kind of strong, long-term government support is crucial for building local manufacturing capabilities and ensuring that next-generation technologies can scale from the lab to the factory floor.
Given the rapid advancements and competitive developments in the battery space, where do you see the industry heading in the next 5 years? What are the biggest hurdles that need to be overcome for solid-state batteries to become the mainstream choice?
Yang:
The next five years will be defined by a race to bring next-generation batteries from testing to production. The current slowdown in EV growth isn't just about cost; fundamentally, it's a battery performance problem. For EVs to achieve mass adoption, batteries must deliver predictable range in all temperatures, eliminate safety risks, and offer gasoline-like refueling in minutes, not hours. We firmly believe that solid-state batteries are a key solution to address these issues.
However, for any new technology to become mainstream, it must overcome two hurdles: it must prove consistent performance in the lab and in real life, and it must prove its viability for mass production at a competitive cost. Many are still stuck at the first hurdle. We believe that with proven chemistry, established manufacturing capability, and a clear path to cost parity with conventional batteries, we have a strong plan to clear both.

title: US Steel: Strengthening Supply Chain With $1.9bn Investment
content:
Article
Operations
US Steel: Strengthening Supply Chain With $1.9bn Investment
By
Louise Collins
May 24, 2026
undefined mins
Share
Share
US Steel is expanding supply chains with new investment. Credit: US Steel
US Steel has announced a US$1.9bn investment to build a new facility at Big River Steel Works in Arkansas, advancing vertical integration across operations
United States Steel Corporation has committed US$1.9bn to construct a direct-reduced-iron facility at Big River Steel Works in Osceola, Arkansas. The facility could establish a vertically integrated supply chain linking the company's Minnesota mining operations to its Arkansas
steel production site
.
According to United States Steel Corporation, the project is expected to support roughly 200 full-time employees and 35 full-time contractor roles. The construction phase could create an estimated 2,000 jobs at peak activity.
Nippon Steel acquired United States Steel Corporation in 2025 in a US$14.189bn transaction. US President Donald Trump approved the deal after former US President Joe Biden attempted to block it.
Connecting mine to mill
The new direct-reduced-iron facility will use United States Steel Corporation's 2022 investment in direct-reduced-grade pellet capabilities at its Minnesota Ore Operations Keetac plant. This connection creates a supply chain pathway between iron ore extraction,
electric arc furnace
feedstock production and final steel manufacturing at Big River Steel Works.
United States Steel Corporation selected Big River Steel Works for direct-reduced-iron production after investing more than US$3bn in an earlier expansion at the site. four electric furnaces now operate at the location, providing a supply advantage for Big River's feedstock requirements.
David B. Burritt, President and Chief Executive Officer of United States Steel Corporation, says: "From iron ore in Minnesota to steel production in Arkansas, this US$1.9bn investment strengthens our
ability to create steel
that is truly mined, melted, made in America, from start to finish.
"By vertically integrating DRI production directly at Big River Steel Works, we enhance efficiency, secure our competitive advantage and position US Steel for long-term success. Our partnership with Nippon Steel helped accelerate this investment years sooner than would have otherwise been possible."
David B. Burritt, US Steel President and Chief Executive Officer (Credit: US Steel)
Nippon Steel takes control
Nippon Steel, Japan's largest steelmaker, acquired United States Steel Corporation in June 2025 for US$14.189bn. Former US President Joe Biden blocked the transaction in January 2025 before US President Donald Trump reversed the decision.
The acquisition agreement gave the US government authority to name a board member through a golden share structure. According to the published terms, this arrangement included the ability to veto relocation and other rights.
The agreement included measures on protecting US national security. These provisions covered approximately US$11bn in
capital investments
by 2028 and the revamping of a blast furnace at Gary Works.
According to a briefing published by Nippon Steel at the time of the deal, the investment is to be primarily funded through United States Steel Corporation's enhanced cash generation. Nippon Steel added that if support is required, optimal funding methods will be considered, taking into account shareholder interests and financial soundness.
US Steel's Big River Steel facility in Osceola. (Credit: US Steel)
Integrated production network
United States Steel Corporation states the US$1.9bn
investment
in direct-reduced-iron advances vertical integration across its operations under a single integrated American supply chain. The company says this approach could improve efficiency, quality and supply chain control.
According to United States Steel Corporation, the integration could
enhance the company's
ability to deliver consistent, high-quality steel with greater reliability for its customers. United States Steel Corporation's operations span the United States and Central Europe.
The company produces steel for electric vehicles, generators and transformers. United States Steel Corporation supplies the automotive industry with customers including GM and Stellantis.
The direct-reduced-iron facility represents the first of its kind in the US. The project links mining, feedstock creation and steel production within a controlled supply chain framework owned by a single entity.

Businesses around the world have been forced to adapt to a new way of operating. With constant geopolitical events re-shaping supply chains, leaders have had to move away from operational efficiency and towards building resilience.
Organisations can no longer withstand responding to each event; now, they need to be able to predict volatility in order to avoid it completely or develop a strategy which enables them to cope throughout turbulence.

Navigating volatility
Throughout the last year, ongoing volatility has shaped supply chain operations. US tariffs, inflation, climate change, AI and conflict have all had their impact on how supply chains work. Constantly changing environments have meant that businesses need to prepare for turbulence, creating multiple solutions,
risk mitigation
strategies and stronger relationships.
Through AI, digital tools and supplier relationship management, businesses are forming more resilient supply chains. The implementation of digital twins allows businesses to trial run solutions, without the cost of a failed project. Other organisations have seen the benefit of increased transparency throughout their tiers, helping them gain insights before issues can become a larger disruptor.

Leaders are understanding the need to develop resilience, with an ongoing push for investments into agility in order to avoid succumbing to risk.

title: This Week's Top Five Stories in Supply Chain
content:
Article
Operations
This Week's Top Five Stories in Supply Chain
By
Louise Collins
May 23, 2026
undefined mins
Share
Share
News from IEA has taken one of the top spots for stories on Supply Chain Digital. Credit: IEA
Supply Chain Digital looks a the top stories of the past week, including insights from Gartner, supply chain technology risks and company strikes
IEA: Oil Supply Chain Reserves Almost Entirely Depleted
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz at the end of February did not cause an immediate supply chain failure because hundreds of tankers loaded with Middle Eastern crude were already sailing towards their destinations. These vessels took weeks to reach terminals in Europe and Asia. As they docked and discharged cargo, the existing pipeline of shipments masked the
scale of the disruption
.
That buffer is now exhausted. According to the International Energy Agency's May 2026 Oil Market Report, global oil inventories dropped by 129 million barrels in March and 117 million barrels in April. This is the fastest rate of inventory depletion on record. The IEA released 400 million barrels from its emergency reserves shortly after the US and Israel began the war on Iran but even this intervention has not kept pace with the drawdown.
"That excess supply is now dwindling at a record pace," says Georgi Kantchev from the Wall Street Journal, "with oil executives and analysts predicting that a
harsh reckoning
is set to upend the relative calm in energy markets."
Gartner: Why CSCO Must Shift to Autonomous Business Mindset
At the opening keynote at the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium in Barcelona, Alan O’Keeffe, VP Analyst in
Gartner’s
Supply Chain practice, opened the show by talking about why chief supply chain officers (CSCOs) must prepare for a new era of business in which decision-making and execution increasingly shift from siloed automation to outcome-driven autonomy.
Gartner, a business and technology insights company, welcomed attendees to its show with its opening presentation at the International Barcelona Convention Center, by giving them the knowledge of how autonomous business capabilities are beginning to reshape supply chain strategy and execution, and the distinct implications for supply chains.
The Gartner Supply Chain Practice provides actionable, objective insights for supply chain leaders and their teams, so they can respond to disruption and innovate for the future through leading-edge supply chain management practices.
High-bandwidth memory chips from SK Hynix are powering the next generation of global AI infrastructure. Credit: SK Hynix
Samsung Strike: AI Memory Shortage and Supply Chain Impacts
A labour dispute at Samsung Electronics could disrupt global memory chip distribution networks as 48,000 workers prepare for an 18-day walkout starting 21 May. The action threatens to interrupt production flows at facilities responsible for 36% of worldwide dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) output.
The strike could remove between 3% and 4% of global DRAM supply from circulation, according to Jeff Kim, analyst at KB Securities.
Samsung operates as the primary supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips to artificial intelligence (AI) data centre operators. Any extended production halt could create cascading delays across
technology supply chains
that depend on consistent semiconductor deliveries.
Cyber Breaches Survey is commissioned by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) and the Home Office | Credit: Getty
Global Supply Chains at Risk of Cyber Breaches and Phishing
The latest Cyber Breaches Survey from the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and the Home Office could suggest UK organisations face a widening gap in supply chain security preparedness.
According to the survey, 43% of businesses and 28% of charities reported
experiencing a breach or attack
in the past year.
The data shows a concerning pattern where visibility into third-party risks remains minimal despite attackers increasingly targeting supplier relationships as entry points into larger systems.
Gartner Senior Director Analyst Jan Snoeckx presents at Gartner Supply Chain Symposium in Barcelona (Credit: Gartner)
Gartner: Is ‘Agent Washing’ a Risk to Supply Chain Planning?
As agentic AI continues to transform the supply chain planning landscape, there is a warning from leaders at Gartner that people must be aware of hype and “agent washing”, which are creating real risks for organisations under pressure to deliver results.
Supply chain planning (SCP) leaders who focus on proven use cases, strengthen data and governance foundations and follow a deliberate adoption sequence can improve near-term productivity while preparing for more advanced agentic capabilities over time, attendees learned at the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium in Barcelona.
“SCP leaders should prepare for an agentic AI future, but they need to separate meaningful capability from market noise,” says Jan Snoeckx, Senior Director Analyst in
Gartner’s
Supply Chain practice.
“The priority today is not full autonomy, but building the operational discipline, architectural flexibility and decision frameworks that allow agentic AI to scale as the technology matures.”

title: Supply Chain Concerns Hike Prices for Nintendo Switch 2
content:
Article
Technology
Supply Chain Concerns Hike Prices for Nintendo Switch 2
By
Louise Collins
May 22, 2026
undefined mins
Share
Share
Shuntaro Furukawa, President of Nintendo | Credit: Nintendo
According to Nintendo, the rise of AI is increasing prices for memory chips, resulting in tighter supply chains and increased costs for gaming technology
Memory chip procurement
has become a constraint for gaming console manufacturers. Nintendo and Sony have both adjusted hardware pricing in response to component cost pressures and supply conditions.
Nintendo announced price changes for its Switch 2 console. The US price will move from US$449.99 to US$499.99 and European markets will see the price adjust from €469.99 to €499.99. These changes take effect in September 2026.
"This is in response to various changes in market conditions, which are expected to extend over the medium-to-long term," Nintendo says.
"We understand that pricing changes can be challenging for customers and deeply appreciate the continued enthusiasm of our fans for Nintendo
products and experiences
."
Sony implemented a US$100 price increase for PlayStation hardware in March.
Memory component pricing trends
Memory chip costs doubled during the first quarter of 2026. Forecasts suggest a further 63% increase in the current quarter, attributed to data centre demand.
Capacity expansion efforts are underway among producers and new fabrication facilities require extended lead times before production begins. Tight
supply conditions
could persist until new lines reach operational status.
Consumer electronics manufacturers face allocation challenges.
Smartphones, laptops and gaming
hardware all compete for the same memory components. Gaming console economics have shifted as a result of these procurement constraints.
Nintendo Switch 2 prices are expected to rise in September | Credit: Nintendo
Nintendo adjusts to input costs
Shuntaro Furukawa, President at Nintendo, cited component costs and
currency exchange rates
as factors in the pricing adjustment. During an earnings call, Shuntaro indicated that profitability could remain similar to the previous financial year despite the price changes.
The company has not disclosed specific memory procurement volumes or contract terms. Supply chain visibility remains limited for the console manufacturer as it navigates component availability.
Currency fluctuations add another variable to hardware margins. Exchange rate movements affect both procurement costs and regional pricing strategies.
Isabelle Tomatis, Vice President of Global Marketing at Sony Interactive Entertainment
Sony secures memory allocation
Sony announced price increases for PlayStation 5 consoles and PlayStation Portal. Isabelle Tomatis, Vice President of Global Marketing at Sony Interactive Entertainment, addressed the adjustment in a PlayStation blog post.
"With continued pressures in the global economic landscape, we've made the decision to increase the prices of PS5, PS5 Pro and PlayStation Portal remote player globally," Isabelle says.
"We know that price changes impact our community and after careful evaluation, we found this was a necessary step to ensure we can
continue delivering innovative
, high-quality gaming experiences to players worldwide."
Hiroki Totoki, President and CEO of Sony | Credit: Sony
Sony has locked memory supply contracts for the current financial year. Hiroki Totoki, Chief Executive Officer at Sony, stated during an earnings briefing that elevated pricing could extend into the following year. Hiroki mentioned the company is examining cost reduction opportunities in non-memory areas.
Hardware sales volumes depend on memory procurement at viable price points, according to Hiroki. Profitability is expected to align with the previous year's performance.
Console pricing historically declined as products aged through their lifecycle. The current trend represents a departure from that pattern, with hardware costs increasing rather than decreasing over time.

title: Gartner: Is ‘Agent Washing’ a Risk to Supply Chain Planning?
content:
Article
AI in Supply Chain
Gartner: Is ‘Agent Washing’ a Risk to Supply Chain Planning?
By
Aaron McMillan
May 20, 2026
undefined mins
Share
Share
Gartner Senior Director Analyst Jan Snoeckx presents at Gartner Supply Chain Symposium in Barcelona (Credit: Gartner)
Jan Snoeckx, Senior Director Analyst at Gartner has warned that supply chain leaders risk ‘agent washing’ in Supply Chain Planning Technology Market
As agentic AI continues to transform the supply chain planning landscape, there is a warning from leaders at Gartner that people must be aware of hype and “agent washing”, which are creating real risks for organisations under pressure to deliver results.
Supply chain planning (SCP) leaders who focus on proven use cases, strengthen data and governance foundations and follow a deliberate adoption sequence can improve near-term productivity while preparing for more advanced agentic capabilities over time, attendees learned at the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium in Barcelona.
“SCP leaders should prepare for an agentic AI future, but they need to separate meaningful capability from market noise,” says Jan Snoeckx, Senior Director Analyst in
Gartner’s
Supply Chain practice.
“The priority today is not full autonomy, but building the operational discipline, architectural flexibility and decision frameworks that allow agentic AI to scale as the technology matures.”
Separating market Noise From True Autonomy
Agentic AI is often found at the centre of messaging coming from vendors, as well as executive discussions in SCP. Jan told those in attendance that most of the current agentic capabilities improve user experience through query interpretation, recommendations and conversational support, rather than fundamentally changing decision quality or how decisions are made.
True
autonomous
planning would require the automatic generation of plans, automatic selection of the optimal plan and seamless execution without human intervention.
Most current solutions have not reached that level of end-to-end autonomy, and Gartner believes that vendors claiming end-to-end autonomous supply chain planning before 2027 are overstating what is possible in the near term.
Jan believes that agent washing further obscures those differences by relabelling conventional automation as agentic, increasing the risk of misaligned investments and long-term lock-in.
Alan O'Keeffe, VP Analyst, Gartner, presents the Opening Keynote at Gartner Supply Chain Symposium in Barcelona
Mitigating risks and avoiding common missteps
Despite current constraints, there are immediate opportunities for
efficiency
gains.
Traditional automation remains well suited to repetitive, low-complexity tasks, while current AI agents can support high-volume, medium-complexity planning actions where risk is low. Gartner recommends a measured approach that captures value now while building the foundations for more advanced agentic planning in the future.​​​​​​​
Jan warned SCP leaders to avoid common missteps in agentic AI adoption:
Do not mistake vendor positioning for true autonomy: Organisations should rigorously scrutinise agentic claims, because many current offerings do not independently re-sequence objectives, negotiate trade-offs or adapt execution logic.
Avoid monolithic transformations and legacy retrofits: Inflexible upgrades and retrofitted agents can limit future flexibility, cap ROI and increase long-term lock-in.
Do not pursue high-risk autonomous use cases too early: Cross-enterprise negotiation, dynamic cost trade-offs and ethical judgment are poor candidates for agentic AI before 2027.
A roadmap for strategic AI integration
According to Gartner research, supply chain planning leaders should take the following actions when evaluating agentic AI solutions:
Prioritise “sweet spot” use cases for immediate value:
Focus early efforts on well-defined, high-volume planning activities where impact is measurable and the cost of error is low, such as touchless forecasting for stable SKUs or automated replenishment parameter changes.
Build data, integration and governance foundations:
Invest in unified, real-time data, robust integration across planning and execution systems and transparent governance with clear guardrails, human hand-off points and audit mechanisms.
Apply frontier AI beyond assistants:
Use AI not only for conversational support, but also to create and maintain digital twins, automate data management and integration and improve how users engage with planning decisions and trade-offs.

title: Gartner: Confidence Gaps in AI Operational Redesign

Gartner: Confidence Gaps in AI Operational Redesign

Louise Collins

Share
Share
Only 36% of Chief Procurement Officers (CPOs) are very confident in their ability to redesign roles and processes around AI (Credit: Getty Images)
Gartner revealed a productivity gap as individual AI gains fail to translate into team-level improvements, with low confidence in restructuring operations
A productivity disconnect is emerging between individual AI users and broader supply chain teams. According to Gartner, only 36% of
Chief Procurement Officers
show high confidence in their capacity to restructure roles and workflows around AI technologies.
The finding came from research presented at the Gartner Supply Chain Symposium/Xpo.
The survey polled 101 CPOs during January and February 2026. Results were shared with attendees at the International Barcelona Convention Centre between May 18 and 20.
The event is considered one of the world's major gatherings for Chief Supply Chain Officers (CSCOs) and supply chain executives. Three-day discussions covered
disruption prediction
, visibility achievement and leadership through AI and innovation.
The AI productivity paradox
According to the Gartner survey,
gen AI deployments
in procurement could improve individual productivity across time savings, output volume and quality. Those results drop substantially when measured at team output level.
Gartner calls this gap the AI productivity paradox. The disconnect exists because procurement operating models have not adapted quickly enough to reflect the effect of gen AI on existing roles.
When AI automates part of a role, the individual may gain productivity. The organisation does not automatically capture the same benefit unless work is restructured across the function.
Fareen Mehrzai, Senior Director Analyst in Gartner's Supply Chain practice, says: "Procurement teams are seeing productivity gains from gen AI, but without intentional redesign of roles and processes, those gains remain confined to the individual level."
Redesigning roles for financial outcomes
Fareen told attendees that CPOs must design next-generation human roles focused on
guiding AI toward
financial outcomes rather than efficiency gains alone. This approach could improve returns on AI investments and unlock organisational gains.
According to Fareen, traditional productivity measurements focused on output-per-unit of time are increasingly misaligned with a modern, AI-enabled procurement function. To maximise gen AI value, CPOs must evolve productivity measures to capture innovative outputs and new sources of value.
Gartner Senior Director Analyst Fareen Mehrzai presents at Gartner Supply Chain Symposium in Barcelona (Credit: Gartner)
Next-generation human roles take on more complex and cognitively demanding tasks in this model. The shift moves away from measuring simple efficiency metrics.
Gartner describes this restructuring as necessary for organisations to realise the full potential of their
AI investments
. Individual productivity gains do not automatically translate to enterprise-level improvements without intentional redesign.
Recommendations for procurement leaders
Gartner shared recommendations for CPOs to redesign
procurement roles
and processes for AI productivity. Fareen outlined a roadmap for next-generation procurement.
The recommendations include evaluating current procurement roles and identifying common tasks. CPOs should separate work into innately human tasks and AI-native tasks.
AI gains should align with financial outcomes. This means focusing on cost optimisation and revenue growth rather than relying solely on efficiency metrics.
Productivity measures need updating to expand performance measures. These should capture innovation, complexity and new outputs created through AI-enabled work.

title: Samsung Strike: AI Memory Shortage and Supply Chain Impacts
content:
Article
Technology
Samsung Strike: AI Memory Shortage and Supply Chain Impacts
By
Louise Collins
May 19, 2026
undefined mins
Share
Share
Samsung is the world's largest memory chipmaker, commanding a dominant 36% share of the global DRAM market. Credit: Samsung
Samsung Electronics is facing an 18-day strike from 48,000 workers, threatening to disrupt global memory chip supplies and remove DRAM from circulation
A labour dispute at Samsung Electronics could disrupt global memory chip distribution networks as 48,000 workers prepare for an 18-day walkout starting 21 May. The action threatens to interrupt production flows at facilities responsible for 36% of worldwide dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) output.
The strike could remove between 3% and 4% of global DRAM supply from circulation, according to Jeff Kim, analyst at KB Securities.
Samsung operates as the primary supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips to artificial intelligence (AI) data centre operators. Any extended production halt could create cascading delays across
technology supply chains
that depend on consistent semiconductor deliveries.
Samsung’s new sixth-generation HBM4 designed for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform. Credit: Samsung Electronics
Disruption to production networks
Samsung runs its memory fabrication across multiple South Korean sites including Pyeongtaek and Hwaseong. These facilities operate continuously across three shifts to maintain wafer output. Nearly 48,000 unionised workers plan to leave production lines on 21 May, representing 38% of the company's domestic workforce.
A South Korean court partially granted an injunction request from Samsung, ruling that essential staffing levels must be maintained during the walkout.
However, a one-day labour action in April showed the vulnerability of semiconductor manufacturing to workforce disruptions. Foundry output dropped 58% and memory fabrication fell 18% during that affected shift, according to industry reports.
The company has begun warm-down procedures to scale back wafer inputs before Thursday. Extended shutdowns force chipmakers to scrap ultra-sensitive silicon wafers worth US$20,000 each. The planned 18-day stoppage represents the largest work disruption in
semiconductor industry
history.
Samsung accounts for nearly a quarter of exports from South Korea. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan tells parliament that citizens are worried about ripple effects across the economy.
High-bandwidth memory chips from SK Hynix are powering the next generation of global AI infrastructure. Credit: SK Hynix
The impacts on buyers
The memory chip shortage arrives as AI infrastructure deployment
maintains demand
at elevated levels.
Samsung supplies DRAM and high-bandwidth memory chips to data centre operators building computing capacity for machine learning workloads. Any supply interruption could delay equipment installations and push up procurement costs for technology buyers.
According to Jeff Kim, NAND flash memory supplies could decline by 2% to 3% if the strike proceeds as planned. Memory chip buyers typically maintain inventory buffers to absorb short-term supply shocks. An 18-day production halt could exhaust those reserves and force purchasers to compete for limited stock from alternative suppliers.
SK Hynix operates as the world's second-largest memory chipmaker after Samsung. The company's production lines could absorb some demand if
Samsung's output
falls. However, SK Hynix already runs fabrication facilities near capacity to meet existing orders for AI hardware.
The supply disruption comes as
semiconductor prices
begin recovering from a downturn in 2024. Further constraints on memory chip availability could fuel price increases across technology supply chains.
Bonus dispute triggers walkout
The National Union of Samsung Electronics is demanding changes to compensation structures that limit performance bonuses to 50% of annual salaries. Workers point to SK Hynix, which overhauled its pay system last year by removing a 10-year cap on bonus payments and allocating 10% of annual operating profit to worker bonuses.
Based on 2026 profit forecasts, SK Hynix employees could receive average payouts from US$460,000 to US$477,000 this year. Samsung paid no performance bonuses in 2024 as its chip unit posted operating losses during the memory downturn. The unit returned to profit in Q1 2026, with operating income increasing nearly eightfold.
The union wants Samsung to abolish the 50% bonus cap and allocate 15% of annual operating profit to a bonus pool. Samsung management proposed a one-off bonus exceeding levels that SK Hynix workers receive this year. However, the company refuses to permanently remove the bonus ceiling from contracts.
The dispute widened after SK Hynix workers received performance bonuses more than three times higher than Samsung employees last year. The compensation gap fuelled discontent at Samsung facilities despite the chip unit's financial recovery.
The wider implications
An anonymous official at South Korea's central bank says the walkout could reduce 0.5 percentage points from a forecast 2.0% expansion in the national economy this year. This assumes approximately 30tn won (US$19.9bn) of chip production could be lost during the stoppage.
Samsung faces competitive pressure from SK Hynix, which is approaching a US$1tn market valuation. SK Hynix supplies high-bandwidth memory chips to AI hardware manufacturers and has secured contracts with major technology buyers. Any extended production disruption at Samsung could shift market share to its domestic rival.
The company held 36% of the global DRAM market at the end of last year, according to industry data. Maintaining that position depends on consistent output from South Korean fabrication facilities. The strike arrives at a time when memory chip buyers have limited alternatives for high-volume procurement.
Samsung must resolve the compensation dispute to restore normal production flows. The company's role in
global semiconductor distribution
networks means any extended supply interruption could affect technology buyers across multiple industries.

title: IEA: Oil Supply Chain Reserves Almost Entirely Depleted
content:
Article
Supply Chain Risk Management
IEA: Oil Supply Chain Reserves Almost Entirely Depleted
By
Louise Collins
May 19, 2026
undefined mins
Share
Share
Ras Laffan Industrial City is the world's largest LNG production hub. Credit: Matthew Smith
The buffer of oil shipments that masked the Strait of Hormuz closure has run dry, leaving global supply chains facing their largest inventory depletion
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz at the end of February did not cause an immediate supply chain failure because hundreds of tankers loaded with Middle Eastern crude were already sailing towards their destinations. These vessels took weeks to reach terminals in Europe and Asia. As they docked and discharged cargo, the existing pipeline of shipments masked the
scale of the disruption
.
That buffer is now exhausted. According to the International Energy Agency's May 2026 Oil Market Report, global oil inventories dropped by 129 million barrels in March and 117 million barrels in April. This is the fastest rate of inventory depletion on record. The IEA released 400 million barrels from its emergency reserves shortly after the US and Israel began the war on Iran but even this intervention has not kept pace with the drawdown.
"That excess supply is now dwindling at a record pace," says Georgi Kantchev from the Wall Street Journal, "with oil executives and analysts predicting that a
harsh reckoning
is set to upend the relative calm in energy markets."
Logistics infrastructure under pressure
The waterway's closure cut off 20% of global fuel supplies, or more than 14 million barrels per day from the Gulf. According to the IEA, supply losses from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the UAE, Kuwait, Iran and Qatar have reached 14.4 million barrels per day below pre-war levels. Total losses from the Gulf's oil producers have already exceeded 1 billion barrels.
The distribution network has been forced to adapt. Saudi Arabia ramped up shipments through its East-West Pipeline, redirecting exports from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea. The UAE pushed more oil through the Fujairah pipeline to avoid the blockage at the Strait of Hormuz.
These pipelines have finite capacity. The volume of oil that can be rerouted through alternative infrastructure falls far short of normal throughput via the Strait. Qatar's Ras Laffan production facility, one of the world's largest oil and gas production hubs, was severely damaged by Iranian airstrikes in March. QatarEnergy has warned that some repairs could take several years to complete. The firm's Mesaieed facility also sustained critical damage.
A graph showing the change in oil supplies over the past five years. Credit: IEA / Wall Street Journal
Even if the Strait of Hormuz were to reopen in June, the IEA projects that global oil supply will average just above 100 million barrels per day across 2026. That is a decline of 3.9 million barrels per day year on year.
The logistics challenge extends beyond crude oil itself. Refined products including diesel, jet fuel and petrol that normally flow from Gulf refineries have also been disrupted, creating secondary bottlenecks in downstream
supply chains
.
Alternative supply routes activated
Producers in the Americas have increased output to compensate. The US hit a record crude output of 14 million barrels per day in April. Brazil notched its third consecutive production record. According to the IEA, exports from the Atlantic Basin have risen by around 3.5 million barrels a day since February, redirected urgently towards markets east of the Suez Canal that have been hardest hit.
The response has not been sufficient. Transportation routes have been lengthened as cargoes travel from the Americas rather than the Gulf. Shipping times from the US Gulf Coast to Asia take several weeks longer than from the Middle East. This extended transit time increases working inventory in the supply chain and delays replenishment cycles.
Global oil stocks are running dangerously low, says the IEA. Credit: IEA
Storage facilities in consuming regions are being depleted faster than they can be refilled. Countries with congested ports and limited storage like Iraq face the most protracted recovery. The IEA notes that it will take two to three months of shipping normalisation before production recovers in earnest, assuming the Strait reopens soon.
Petrochemical feedstock supply chains have collapsed in parts of Asia. LPG and naphtha demand has fallen sharply as Gulf supplies dried up. India has seen household cooking fuel arrivals drop more than 40% from pre-war levels, causing large queues for LPG cylinders. Industrial users dependent on consistent feedstock flows have reduced production schedules or temporarily shuttered facilities.
Demand destruction across sectors
Consumer behaviour has shifted as prices climbed to a record high of US$144.68 per barrel for North Sea Dated crude in April. This surpassed the 2008 financial crash peak. The IEA now forecasts global oil demand to contract by 420,000 barrels per day year on year in 2026, a reversal of 1.3 million barrels per day from its pre-war forecast.
Aviation logistics have been disrupted. Global Revenue Passenger Kilometres fell 0.6% year on year in March, the first decline in five years. Flights passing over the Middle East were delayed, rerouted or cancelled. Airports in Iran, Iraq and Kuwait remained closed in early May.
Some Middle Eastern countries, like Saudi Arabia, have made use of pipelines to reroute exports that would normally travel through the Strait of Hormuz. Credit: Aramco
Motorists around the world responded with panic buying. UK petrol stations saw surges in sales of around 39% in early March. This created temporary spikes in retail demand that strained local distribution networks. Pakistan, the Philippines and Sri Lanka have introduced four-day working weeks. Other nations in Southeast Asia have implemented work from home mandates
to save energy
.
"If the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed and commercial oil inventories continue to be drawn down at their recent pace, that would be consistent with Brent crude oil prices rising towards record highs this summer," says Hamad Hussain, Climate and Commodities Economist at Capital Economics.
Hamad Hussain, Climate and Commodities Economist at Capital Economics. Credit: Hamad Hussain
The war is now in its twelfth week and peace talks remain unaligned. The US Department of Defense has acknowledged that clearing sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz could alone take months. The total global
oil deficit
is projected to reach 900 million barrels by September 2026.
According to the IEA, rebuilding depleted stocks would require approximately one million barrels per day of surplus supply for the next three years, on top of underlying demand growth. The market is expected to remain in deficit until at least the fourth quarter of this year. North Sea Dated was trading around US$110 per barrel at the time of writing.
The supply chain cushion that absorbed the initial shock has been exhausted. Restocking global inventories to
pre-war levels
will require sustained surplus production and uninterrupted shipping routes for several years. The logistics network that kept oil flowing after the closure has reached the limits of its capacity to compensate.
